introduction: I’m an A Level student in Riyadh preparing to study law. Aviation got me interested in how teams make decisions, and that curiosity now runs through my work in technology, negotiation and writing.
homeProfile: Aviation was one of my first interests. Independent courses in crew management and aircraft design gave me a closer look at how people coordinate, communicate and make decisions under pressure.
That led me towards business and commercial law. I’m particularly curious about what happens when companies buy, sell or invest in a business, and how they decide who takes on the risk.

biography: I’m a Pakistani student living in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. I completed my IGCSEs at Al-Rowad International Schools, where I now study Mathematics, Physics and Computer Science at International A Level. I expect to finish in 2028.

Aviation was one of my first interests. Studying crew management and aircraft design made me curious about the decisions and coordination behind a flight. I’ve since explored business and technology through short courses and events in Riyadh.
interests: I’m an avid reader and am currently working on The Eleventh Rehearsal, a psychological thriller about memory and the stories people tell about the past.
I’m interested in how companies make decisions, particularly when acquiring a business or using new technology. That’s part of what draws me to corporate and commercial law.

projects.title: UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI
projects.description: At the fourth UNESCO forum in Riyadh, I listened to how countries and organisations were putting AI ethics into practice. I left thinking about who is accountable once AI starts shaping real decisions.

image.alt: Delegates gathered beneath a chandelier at the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI in Riyadh.
image.caption: Forum delegates in Riyadh. Photo by the Saudi Press Agency.

homeImage.alt: A panel speaking in front of an audience at the UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI in Riyadh.

body: I went to the fourth UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI expecting something closer to LEAP. I thought I would spend most of the day seeing what the latest tools could do. Instead, I listened to people from governments, international organisations, research and industry work through what should happen when those tools are put to use. It was the first edition of the forum held in the Gulf. UNESCO reported more than 10,000 participants and delegations from over 50 Member States across the event in Riyadh.

sections.title: Who takes responsibility?
paragraphs: The question I kept coming back to was who has to answer when AI causes harm. Think of a company using software to screen applicants. If the software rejects someone unfairly, the company needs to know who can explain what happened, who can review the decision and who can put it right. The answers get more complicated when the company, the vendor and the people affected are in different countries. The forum made the practical side of human oversight easier for me to see.

sections.title: From principles to implementation
paragraphs: I learned more about UNESCO’s 2021 Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. It gives countries a shared framework for issues such as privacy, transparency, human oversight and fair treatment. One development at the forum was RAM 2.0, an updated readiness assessment that helps countries identify gaps in their laws, institutions and technical capacity. UNESCO also released a synthesis of 55 country reports. These tools made it easier to see how governments can turn a broad commitment into work they can actually measure.

sections.title: The resources behind the technology
paragraphs: I had mostly thought about AI ethics through the decisions a system makes about people. The environmental discussions gave me another set of questions to consider. Scaling AI can put pressure on electricity, water and other resources, and those costs also have to be part of decisions about deployment. UNESCO launched a toolkit at the forum to help policymakers account for those impacts.

sections.title: Conversations beyond the sessions
paragraphs: I spoke with people from different countries and backgrounds between sessions. Those conversations helped me understand why a shared framework can matter even when countries have different priorities. Some are deciding how to supervise systems they already rely on. Others are still building the institutions and skills they would need to do that. Hearing how people approached those questions was one of the most memorable parts of the day.

sections.title: What I took away for corporate law
paragraphs: My interest in corporate law gave me another way into the discussion. When a business brings an AI system into its operations, there are questions about what data the vendor can use, who can investigate a problem and what the company has agreed to do when something goes wrong. I left wanting to understand how businesses and governments turn ethical commitments into decisions people can review and challenge.

projects.title: Lead & Influence: Negotiation and Communication Workshop
projects.description: I completed the two-day Essentials Workshop, practising public speaking and negotiation through exercises and simulations.
projects.workSummary: I worked on making a point clearly, then listening for what the other person needed before deciding where there was room to negotiate.

image.alt: Nicholas Coburn-Palo speaking into a microphone on stage at Harvard Business School.
image.caption: Nicholas Coburn-Palo speaking about strategic listening at Harvard Business School’s Lectures that Last event. Photo from his public LinkedIn post.

body: I took NY Empire Academy’s two-day Essentials Workshop with Nicholas Coburn-Palo, a preceptor in public speaking at Harvard University, and Kate Clark. The format gave me time to practise both delivering a clear message and listening carefully to the person across the table.

sections.title: Public speaking
paragraphs: The speaking exercises gave me a chance to organise my points before delivering them. I practised making the main point clear and giving the listener enough context to follow it.

sections.title: Negotiation
paragraphs: In the simulations I practised explaining my position and listening for the other side’s priorities. Hearing what mattered to them helped me think about which parts of a proposal had room to move.

projects.title: Graduation ceremony volunteering
projects.description: I helped set up the ceremony, seat guests and support backstage logistics as a student volunteer.
projects.workSummary: I worked alongside staff and other students before guests arrived and during the ceremony. Moving between the guest area and backstage showed me how much a smooth event depends on clear handovers and good timing.
body: I volunteered at Al-Rowad International Schools’ graduation ceremony in May 2025. I worked alongside staff and other students, helping prepare the event space, guiding guests to their seats and lending a hand backstage.

sections.title: Before the ceremony
paragraphs: I helped with setup before guests arrived. Once people began coming in, I guided attendees to their seats so they could get settled before the ceremony started.

sections.title: Behind the scenes
paragraphs: I also supported the backstage team as the ceremony got underway. Working between the guest area and backstage showed me how much a smooth event depends on people keeping each other informed and picking up small tasks as they come up.

projects.title: Designing a personal portfolio
projects.description: I built this site to bring my education, projects and interests together in one place.
projects.workSummary: I organised the material into dedicated pages, revised the writing and checked how the layouts read on phones, tablets and desktops. The project made me more deliberate about what someone needs to see first and what deserves its own page.
body: I shaped the content and design with AI-assisted development. I wanted someone new to the site to be able to find my educational background, explore a project or read my writing without sorting through everything at once.

sections.title: Structuring the site
paragraphs: I gave education, work and writing dedicated spaces. The overview pages offer enough context to decide what to read next, and the detail pages give a project or event room for a proper explanation.

sections.title: Design and review
paragraphs: I revised the typography, images and page layouts across phone, tablet and desktop widths. Reviewing the pages at different sizes helped me spot awkward line breaks and gaps that were easy to miss on a single screen.

projects.title: Money20/20 Middle East
projects.description: I explored agentic commerce and how a company can tell whether an AI agent has permission to make a purchase for someone.
body: Money20/20 brought banks, fintech companies and technology providers together in Riyadh. I went to see how the AI systems I had been following were being used in financial services. I attended a session on agentic commerce and walked through the exhibition, where payment companies and identity and security providers were working on different parts of the same problem.

sections.title: What I took away
paragraphs: An AI agent that can make a purchase still needs a way to prove who it represents and what it is allowed to do. The discussions about moving from pilots to live products made clear how much depends on authentication, reliable infrastructure and the controls available to the customer.

projects.title: LEAP Riyadh
projects.description: I saw robots, autonomous delivery vehicles and palm-based payments demonstrated, and considered what it would take to use them every day.
body: LEAP’s 2026 edition brought startups, established technology companies and investors to Riyadh. I spent time with the exhibits on robotics, autonomous transport and new ways to pay. I also tried an F1 simulator and learned about the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix.

sections.title: What I took away
paragraphs: Seeing the demonstrations gave me a better sense of what is already being tested. It also made me think about what everyday use would demand. A driverless delivery vehicle has to handle changing streets and unexpected obstacles, and a palm payment system has to protect the biometric data that makes it work.

projects.title: Black Hat Middle East & Africa

eventLogo.alt: Black Hat Middle East & Africa logo

projects.description: I attended cybersecurity workshops and briefings in Riyadh and completed ten hours of continuing professional development.
body: Black Hat MEA brought security researchers, practitioners and technology providers together for workshops and briefings. I joined sessions on emerging threats and approaches to defending systems. I completed ten hours of CPD activities and received a certificate for ten CPD credits.

sections.title: What I took away
paragraphs: The workshops helped me see how a team goes from understanding a threat to deciding what it can do about it. The discussions also gave me a clearer picture of how security affects decisions across an organisation, from the tools people use to how they respond when something goes wrong.

projects.title: Global Airports Forum
projects.description: I spoke with aviation professionals about airport operations and acquired a metal collectible from a retired Emirates Airbus A380.
body: The forum brought airport operators, technology providers and aviation professionals to Riyadh. I met people working across different parts of the industry and heard how they manage airport operations. A short boarding delay offered a useful example. It can affect gate availability, baggage handling and the aircraft’s next flight, so several teams may need to adjust their plans together.

sections.title: What I took away
paragraphs: I became interested in how airports can use AI to anticipate delays and manage passenger flow. A prediction is useful when the teams involved can act on it, and the forum helped me see how much coordination sits behind decisions that look simple from the terminal.

sections.title: A piece of a retired Emirates A380
paragraphs: I also acquired a metal collectible cut from the vertical stabiliser of a retired Emirates Airbus A380. The vertical stabiliser is the upright part of the tail. It was striking to hold a piece of an aircraft that size and know exactly where on the airframe it came from.

writingPractice: I’m an avid reader and I write fiction. This novel lets me explore how much of what we remember comes from stories we’ve heard over and over.

writing.title: The Eleventh Rehearsal
writing.description: The voice on the tape is his. So why does the story sound rehearsed?
synopsis: Daniel Vane edits sound for a living. He knows how much can disappear in four seconds, and how easy it is to leave a sentence that sounds whole. For seventeen years, he’s lived with a version of the night his mother vanished that has always seemed complete.

Then a file arrives from Bellwether, the country house where she worked. There’s an appointment he never agreed to and a recording he doesn’t remember making. He recognises his own voice. It’s the pause before he speaks that unnerves him.

Back in Mereford, Daniel starts to compare what he remembers with what other people kept. A voice has been edited. A photograph has changed. And the people offering to help him remember seem remarkably sure what he ought to say. Before he can work out what happened that night, he has to ask a harder question: who taught him how to tell it?
body: Daniel Vane edits sound for a living. Seventeen years after his mother vanished, a file from Bellwether arrives with a recording in his own voice and an appointment he never agreed to.
Back in Mereford, Daniel listens for what the records leave out. The closer he gets to the night she disappeared, the harder it becomes to trust the version he’s lived with.
